coverageDimensions:
SERVICE COVERAGE — would mean: of the AWS services that exist, how many does Security Hub CSPM ship at least one control for. The page gives this only by INFERENCE, and says so obliquely: the intro states the control ID "indicates the AWS service and resource that the control relates to". Splitting the 589 IDs on the dot yields 82 distinct prefix strings and 81 distinct services once you fold the casing bug (both "AutoScaling.1/.2/.3/.6/.9/.10" and "Autoscaling.5" appear — one service, two spellings). Even at 81 this is not a clean service list: prefixes are informal, not AWS service names (ES and Opensearch are two prefixes for what is now one service; DataFirehose, PCA, IVS, Keyspaces, ELB, ES are abbreviations needing a lookup table the page does not supply). Density is very uneven — EC2 65, RDS 49, IAM 27, SageMaker 25, S3 21, ELB 18, ECS 17, CloudWatch 17, Redshift 16, CloudFront 15 — so "has a control" is a weak claim. And there is NO denominator and NO not-covered list: the page never states which AWS services Security Hub has no controls for. Verdict: a derived numerator of 81, no denominator, no exclusions. Do not publish a service percentage from this page.

REGION COVERAGE — would mean: for each control, in which AWS Regions is it available, or which Regions run the full 589. THE PAGE GIVES YOU NOTHING. The word "Region" appears on this page only inside control TITLES (CloudTrail.1 "multi-Region trail", S3.7 "cross-Region replication", S3.24 "S3 Multi-Region Access Points") — that is subject matter, not availability. There is no Region column, no Region footnote, no availability caveat anywhere. Security Hub does publish controls that are not supported in every Region, but that lives on a different page. Any Region claim sourced from this page is fabricated.

RESOURCE TYPE COVERAGE — would mean: which resource types (AWS::EC2::SecurityGroup, AWS::S3::Bucket, and so on) Security Hub CSPM evaluates. THE PAGE GIVES YOU ESSENTIALLY NOTHING USABLE. The intro claims the control ID indicates the service "and resource", but no column carries a resource type, no CloudFormation-style or ARN-style type identifier appears anywhere, and the second ID segment is a bare sequence number, not a resource. Resource nouns exist only inside free-text titles ("SNS topics", "EC2 instances", "Transfer Family connectors"), which would require NLP guessing and would still be undercounted (many controls target a configuration, not a type) and overcounted (one control can name two types). There is no enumerable resource-type set and no not-supported set. Verdict: no resource-type coverage from this page.

What the page DOES give cleanly: standard coverage (10 standards, external axis, per-control membership counted) and two within-catalogue capability splits (custom parameters 190/399, schedule type 447 change-triggered / 149 periodic).

features.featureName: Security Hub CSPM controls (the control reference table)
features.reasoning: Security controls are what this page exists to enumerate, and a control ID is Security Hub's own identifier for its own check. That makes the axis a catalogue: Security Hub holds 100% of its own control list by construction, so "589 of 589 = 100% coverage" is a tautology and must never be rendered as a coverage ratio. The 589 number is still valuable — as a denominator for the three real Yes/No claims below, and as a raw size figure — but never as a numerator over itself.
features.statuses: 589 rows, 589 distinct control IDs, zero duplicates. All 589 are stated as supported by their mere presence: the intro says only controls "in active use" are listed. The not-covered side is stated but NOT enumerable: "Retired controls are excluded from the table" names a category with no members on the page, so the count of not-covered values is 0-listable, not 0-existing. The prose also warns "Control IDs may skip numbers. These are placeholders for future controls" — the gaps (APIGateway.6/7, AppSync.1/3, WAF.5/9) are not retired controls and must not be inferred as anything.

features.reasoning: CIS AWS Foundations Benchmark, NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, NIST SP 800-171 Rev. 2 and PCI DSS are third-party compliance frameworks that exist whether or not Security Hub does, which makes the axis external and the ratio meaningful. Two of the ten (AWS Foundational Security Best Practices, AWS Resource Tagging Standard) are AWS-published, so the axis is not purely external — but eight of ten are, and the useful question ("does Security Hub cover PCI DSS v4.0.1?") is an external one. Critical honesty caveat: this list is DERIVED from the column values, not declared. The page never says "these are the standards Security Hub supports". A standard that Security Hub supports but that currently has zero active controls would be invisible here. Treat 10 as "standards reachable from this page", not "all standards Security Hub supports".
features.scope: per security control — this column is a 589 x 10 membership matrix, not a flat list
features.statuses: 10 distinct standards, all covered (each has at least one control). Per-control membership counted off the page: AWS Foundational Security Best Practices v1.0.0 = 376; NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 = 298; PCI DSS v4.0.1 = 142; AWS Resource Tagging Standard = 137; NIST SP 800-171 Rev. 2 = 63; PCI DSS v3.2.1 = 44; CIS AWS Foundations Benchmark v1.2.0 = 42; CIS AWS Foundations Benchmark v5.0.0 = 40; CIS AWS Foundations Benchmark v1.4.0 = 39; CIS AWS Foundations Benchmark v3.0.0 = 37. Total 1218 memberships. Not-covered is stated only cell by cell (a control's absence from a standard's list), never as a named exclusion. Exactly one control has a BLANK standards cell — EC2.22, "Unused EC2 security groups should be removed" — so it belongs to zero of the 10. Three source defects must be normalised before counting: (a) FSBP is written two ways, "AWS Foundational Security Best Practices v1.0.0" (167 rows) and "AWS Foundational Security Best Practices" (208 rows) — same standard, so raw distinct-value counting yields 11, not 10; (b) CloudTrail.2 is missing a comma, giving the literal token "CIS AWS Foundations Benchmark v1.4.0 AWS Foundational Security Best Practices v1.0.0"; (c) one row lists CIS v3.0.0 twice.

features.reasoning: This is the cleanest true coverage claim on the page: a named capability (custom values for control parameters) that demonstrably reaches some controls and demonstrably does not reach others, with AWS stating both sides in a column. The axis is a catalogue — Security Hub's own controls — but unlike the catalogue's own existence, the 190/589 (32.3%) ratio is meaningful, because it is a real partition inside the catalogue rather than a count of a set against itself. Present it as "190 of 589 controls support custom parameters", never as "Security Hub covers 32% of anything".
features.statuses: An explicit Yes/No column rendered as icon-yes.png/icon-no.png plus the word. Yes = 190 controls, No = 399 controls. 190 + 399 = 589, so every row is decided and none is blank or unknown.

features.reasoning: This is the page's per-scan-method dimension. As three labels it is a classification, not coverage; but decomposed into the two underlying evaluation methods it becomes a genuine reaches / does-not-reach claim over the control catalogue, and the combined value proves the two methods are independent rather than mutually exclusive. Include it only in the decomposed form — a parser that treats "Change triggered and periodic" as a third method invents a capability AWS does not name.
features.statuses: Three literal values: "Change triggered" = 440 controls, "Periodic" = 142 controls, "Change triggered and periodic" = 7 controls. 440 + 142 + 7 = 589, every row decided. Read as two evaluation methods rather than three labels: change-triggered evaluation reaches 447 controls (440 + 7) and does not reach 142; periodic evaluation reaches 149 controls (142 + 7) and does not reach 440.

pageTitle: Control reference for Security Hub CSPM
shouldNotExtract: 1. SEVERITY. Four values — CRITICAL 29, HIGH 74, MEDIUM 284, LOW 202 — but severity is a property a control HAS, not a thing a capability REACHES. It fits no coverage sentence. Keep it as row metadata or drop it; never as an axis. 2. The "See also" section, whose only content is the AI-coding-assistant boilerplate AWS now appends to every page ("Skills for AI coding assistants (optional)... aws agent-toolkit search-skills"). It is not a capability, and the Agent Toolkit is not a coverage axis. 3. The six column-definition bullets in the intro. They describe the table; they are not six capabilities and not six values. 4. Every inline link target — controls-findings-create-update.md, custom-control-parameters.md, automations.md, asff-changes-consolidation.md, securityhub-standards-schedule.md, and the 589 per-service control pages (account-controls.md, acm-controls.md, ...). These are navigation. The 82 distinct linked filenames are especially tempting as a "supported services" list and must not be taken as one. 5. The icon image URLs (images/icon-yes.png, images/icon-no.png). Read the Yes/No word; the URL is presentation. 6. Control-ID number gaps. APIGateway skips 6 and 7, AppSync skips 1 and 3, WAF skips 5 and 9, EC2 numbering is sparse. AWS states these are "placeholders for future controls". They are not retired controls, not unsupported items, and not values of any axis. 7. The anchor tag and the H1 itself as data. 8. The word "deprecated" inside CloudFront.10's title ("should not use deprecated SSL protocols") — that describes what the control checks, not the control's own status.
trap:
The headline trap is publishing "Security Hub CSPM: 589 of 589 controls covered, 100%". The control list is Security Hub's own catalogue; it holds all of it by definition, and the intro has already removed the only interesting negatives ("Retired controls are excluded from the table"). The real not-covered set exists and is deliberately invisible, so a 100% figure is a tautology dressed as a result.

Second, and almost as likely: counting distinct Applicable-standards strings and reporting 11. AWS writes the same standard two ways in the same column — "AWS Foundational Security Best Practices v1.0.0" (167 rows) and "AWS Foundational Security Best Practices" (208 rows). A naive splitter also produces the corrupt token "CIS AWS Foundations Benchmark v1.4.0 AWS Foundational Security Best Practices v1.0.0" from CloudTrail.2, where AWS dropped a comma, and will double-count CIS v3.0.0 on the one row that lists it twice. Normalise, then the answer is 10.

Third: deriving services from ID prefixes and reporting 82, missing that "AutoScaling" (6 controls) and "Autoscaling" (1 control, AutoScaling.5) are the same service. The correct derived figure is 81 — and it should not be presented as coverage at all, because the page supplies no denominator and no unsupported-service list.

Fourth: treating "Change triggered and periodic" (7 controls) as a third evaluation method, which invents a capability, instead of as membership in both.

Fifth: silently dropping EC2.22, the one control whose Applicable standards cell is empty. A parser that skips blank cells loses a real fact — this control belongs to zero of the ten standards.

Sixth: claiming anything about Regions. The page contains no availability data whatsoever, and the word "Region" appears only inside control titles as subject matter.
whatThePageStates: This page is a single flat reference table of every AWS Security Hub CSPM control that is in active use, one row per control, sorted by control ID. It has six columns: Security control ID, Security control title, Applicable standards, Severity, Supports custom parameters, and Schedule type. The intro prose explains each column and states one exclusion up front: "Only controls in active use by Security Hub CSPM are included here. Retired controls are excluded from the table." There is exactly one table, no Topics block, no footnotes, and no Note/Important callouts. The only other heading is "See also", which holds nothing but the AI-coding-assistant boilerplate.
